  5. Longevity through "good enough" simplicity.
  VT100 escape codes covered cursor movement, screen clearing, basic text attributes (bold,
  underline, reverse video), and later color extensions, which was sufficient for the vast
  majority of text-based UI needs for decades. There was rarely enough pressure to displace
  it with something fundamentally different, because incremental extensions (256-color codes,
  true-color codes, mouse reporting, bracketed paste) could all be layered onto the existing
  escape-sequence framework without breaking backward compatibility. Nobody had to rewrite
  the world; they just had to add more sequences to the same namespace.

  In short: VT100 won not because it was the best terminal on pure technical merit in 1978,
  but because it sat at the intersection of a real ANSI standard, DEC's massive market
  presence during Unix's formative years, and a self-reinforcing compatibility chain through
  termcap/terminfo and software emulators like xterm. Once enough software assumed VT100
  semantics, un-assuming it became more expensive than any competing scheme was worth, and
  that asymmetry, more than any single design virtue, is why those codes are still what your
  terminal speaks today.
